literal: His father was Yizong.
idiomatic: His father was Yizong.

literal: Bao's physique was lofty and imposing; his voice and bearing were fine.
idiomatic: Bao was tall and broad-shouldered, with a handsome voice and bearing.

literal: Upon doffing the hemp he became an opening-office staff officer, concurrently mobile-office gentleman, and followed Murong Shaozong.
idiomatic: He doffed the hemp and entered service as an opening-office staff officer and concurrent mobile-office gentleman, attending Murong Shaozong.

literal: Shaozong said himself that he had a water bane; he therefore bathed in the war galley and also threw himself into the water, hoping to use repellence to meet and counter it.
idiomatic: Shaozong claimed a water bane was upon him, so he bathed aboard the war galley and even threw himself into the river, hoping an apotropaic counter-measure would turn fate aside.

literal: Bao said, "Fate lies in Heaven—can human reason shorten or lengthen it?
idiomatic: Bao said, "Fate is Heaven's to give—what mortal scheme could hurry or delay it?

literal: If my lord truly has disaster and bane, I fear averting rites cannot resolve it;
idiomatic: If you truly face disaster, I doubt any averting rite can lift it;

literal: if in truth there is none, what is there to avert?
idiomatic: if there is none in truth, what would you avert?

literal: " Shaozong laughed and said, "One cannot escape vulgar custom—for a little while one does the same again.
idiomatic: " Murong Shaozong laughed. "Cannot escape the vulgar," he said; "one goes through the motions, that is all.

literal: " Before long Shaozong met drowning; commentators of the time held that Bao had known the subtle sign.
idiomatic: " Before long Murong Shaozong drowned; opinion at the time took it that Bao had read the omen.

literal: He was promoted to Administrator of Leling; he governed with weight and solemnity, pitying the poor and weak.
idiomatic: Promoted to administrator of Leling, he ruled with grave steadiness and pitied the poor and weak.

literal: Under Bao the court and courtyard were plain and quiet; the prisons stood empty.
idiomatic: Under Bao the yamen stayed plain and quiet and the cells stood empty.

literal: The commandery seat lay by the sea; the water tasted mostly salty and bitter. Bao ordered a well dug, and sweet spring was obtained; far and near took it as caused by his transforming governance.
idiomatic: The seat lay on the coast, where the water ran salty and bitter. Bao had a well sunk and sweet water rose; people far and near credited his transforming rule.

literal: After Bao left office and returned home, the well's taste turned salty again.
idiomatic: Once Bao had left office and gone home, the well turned salty again.

literal: When Qi was destroyed, he returned to his home estate to nourish himself; summons came repeatedly, but he pleaded illness and declined.
idiomatic: When Qi fell he went home to tend his estate. Summons came again and again; he pleaded illness and stayed away.

literal: He died at home.
idiomatic: He died at home.

literal: Lu Qubing was a man of Yangping.
idiomatic: Lu Qubing was a native of Yangping.

literal: His spirit and bearing were open and clear; his appearance was singular and striking.
idiomatic: His manner was open and lucid; his looks were singular and striking.

literal: Upon doffing the hemp he became an opening-office staff officer.
idiomatic: He doffed the hemp and became an opening-office staff officer.

literal: An edict ordered that literati be used as county magistrates; Qubing was made Magistrate of Raoyang in Dingzhou.
idiomatic: An edict required that cultivated men serve as county magistrates, and Qubing was appointed magistrate of Raoyang in Dingzhou.

literal: Qubing was clear and adept in affairs of the time; his nature was rather stern and firm—men did not dare deceive him, yet he was utterly fair and incorrupt, and officials and commoners alike sighed in admiration.
idiomatic: Qubing understood the affairs of the age and was by nature stern and firm; none dared cheat him, yet he was utterly fair, and officials and commoners alike marveled.

literal: He was promoted to Magistrate of Cheng'an.
idiomatic: He was promoted to magistrate of Cheng'an.

literal: Near the capital lay three counties—Ye, Linzhang, and Cheng'an. Under the chariot-hub they had long been called hard to govern; compounded by chaotic government and hard times, the net of law was not established, and meritorious ministers and imperial affines made requests from every quarter.
idiomatic: Below the capital stood Ye, Linzhang, and Cheng'an—three counties long notorious under the imperial hub. Disorder piled on hard times; law's net hung slack, and meritorious ministers and imperial kin pressed requests from every side.

literal: Qubing kept himself informed of affairs and answered requests with reason; men of power—even grooms and petty servants—all feared his integrity of style, yet none came to resent him.
idiomatic: Qubing tracked every matter and answered on principle. Men of influence—even grooms and petty servants—feared his bearing, yet none bore him a grudge.

literal: From the move to Ye onward, among the three county magistrates' methods of governance, Qubing alone was ranked first.
idiomatic: After the court moved to Ye, among the three magistrates' ways of rule, Qubing alone was ranked first.

literal: When Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou pacified Qi, he valued their ability in office—Qubing and Gongsun Jingmao, Administrator of Jiyin, were the two not replaced; an edict was issued to praise and commend them.
idiomatic: When Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou conquered Qi, he prized their competence in office. Qubing and Gongsun Jingmao, administrator of Jiyin, were the two not replaced; an edict singled them out for praise.

literal: In the Daye era of Sui, he died while serving as Magistrate of Jishi.
idiomatic: In the Daye era of Sui he died in office as magistrate of Jishi.

literal: The full text uses Zhonghua Shuju, November 1972, first edition Book of Northern Qi, as the base for this collation.
idiomatic: The full text has been collated against Zhonghua Shuju, first edition Book of Northern Qi (November 1972).
